proposal: Lassman argues that tariffs raise consumer prices and invite retaliation, and recommends that a new administration end all tariffs imposed under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 and Sections 201 and 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, then work with Congress to repeal those provisions so future Presidents cannot use them.

status_summary: The administration moved in the opposite direction. On 2025-06-03 it doubled the Section 232 tariff on steel and aluminum to 50 percent (effective 2025-06-04), and the U.S.-EU framework of 2025-08-21 refers to Section 232 tariffs on autos, pharmaceuticals, semiconductors and lumber. When Executive Order 14389 ended the IEEPA tariffs on 2026-02-20, it stated that Section 232 and Section 301 duties were unaffected. In August 2026 new Section 232 proclamations covered polysilicon (Proclamation 11052, effective 2026-12-04) and unmanned aircraft systems (Proclamation 11055, first duties from 2026-09-03), and on 2026-07-23 USTR added new Section 301 tariffs of 10 to 12.5 percent on 60 economies. On 2026-10-07 USTR published a notice that the 2018 Section 301 actions on China remain in effect after domestic industry requested their continuation, with a further review and public comment process to follow. No removal of any Section 232, 201 or 301 action and no repeal bill was found through 2026-10-13.

timeline.event: Proclamation raises the Section 232 additional tariff on steel and aluminum articles and derivatives from 25 to 50 percent effective 2025-06-04 (UK remains at 25 percent).
U.S.-EU framework statement refers to Section 232 tariffs on pharmaceuticals, semiconductors and lumber and on autos, with a 15 percent ceiling for EU goods.
China arrangement extends certain Section 301 tariff exclusions to 2026-11-10, indicating the Section 301 tariffs remain in effect.
Executive Order 14389 ends IEEPA duties but states that Section 232 and Section 301 duties are not affected.
USTR imposes new Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies for failing to adopt forced-labor import bans, at 10 to 12.5 percent.
timeline.source: Office of the U.S. Trade Representative

timeline.event: Proclamation 11052 (published 2026-08-11, 91 FR 51975) adjusts imports of polysilicon and its derivatives under Section 232, setting minimum import prices and an additional 15 percent duty on ingots and derivatives, with all-in rates of 15 percent for several partners and 10 percent for the UK, effective 2026-12-04.

Proclamation 11055 (published 2026-08-19, 91 FR 53699) imposes Section 232 duties of 100 percent and 25 percent on unmanned aircraft systems and some components, with the first duties effective 2026-09-03 and duties on other listed components from 2027-02-09.
USTR statement on Section 338 duties and import bans against Canada.
timeline.source: Office of the U.S. Trade Representative

timeline.event: Commerce (BIS) publishes a temporary final rule (91 FR 60505, effective 2026-09-22 through 2026-12-03) restricting stockpiling of polysilicon imports ahead of the Proclamation 11052 measures.

USTR publishes a notice (91 FR 64212) that, after receiving continuation requests from domestic producers and trade associations in the statutory four-year review, the two 2018 Section 301 actions on China remain in effect, and says it will conduct a review with a public comment process.

A Federal Register API check for presidential documents mentioning Section 232 after 2026-08-01 listed only the polysilicon and unmanned aircraft proclamations and two Canada Section 338 scope modifications of 2026-09-14. A listing of presidential documents from 2026-09-08 through 2026-10-13 showed no tariff proclamation, but its second page was not opened.
